In the WHO global air quality guidelines (2021 update), the recommended AQG levels are:

- **(a) Sulfur dioxide (SO₂), 24-hour mean: 40 µg/m³**, up from 20 µg/m³ in the 2005 guidelines [ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK574591/table/ch3.tab26/). This is defined as the 99th percentile, i.e. 3-4 exceedance days per year.
- **(b) Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), annual mean: 10 µg/m³**, down from 40 µg/m³ in the 2005 guidelines [ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK574591/table/ch3.tab26/).

The same values appear in the WHO guideline document's summary table, which also lists interim targets: 125 and 50 µg/m³ for 24-hour SO₂, and 40, 30 and 20 µg/m³ for annual NO₂ [iris.who.int](https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/b729bbc4-7032-4799-898e-d112faa16f22/content).

**TI = 16, and yes, it is within the limit**, which is 50 for a freight container used as packaging under the current edition, SSR-6 (Rev. 2), 2025 Edition.

**Calculation (para. 523)**

1. Multiply the maximum dose rate at 1 m by 100: 0.08 mSv/h × 100 = 8.
2. Apply the Table 7 size-of-load factor, since a tank or a freight container used as packaging is one of the load types that gets it. For a largest cross-sectional area of 3 m², the factor is 2. I've taken the band (over 1 m² and up to 5 m²) from memory of Table 7, as the search results did not show the table values.
3. TI = 8 × 2 = 16. No rounding is needed.

**Limit check (para. 526)**

- The 2025 edition separates the two cases: an ordinary package or overpack not under exclusive use is still held to 10, because the TI of any package, other than a freight container used as packaging, or any overpack shall not exceed 10.
- Your container falls under the other limb, where the cap is higher: the TI of any freight container used as packaging shall not exceed 50.
- So 16 is below 50, and the container can travel without exclusive use on TI grounds. Exclusive use would only be triggered with an individual TI greater than 50.

**Edition matters here.** The 2018 edition (SSR-6 Rev. 1) has no separate provision for freight containers used as packaging, and as I recall it the general package limit of 10 applied. On that reading, a TI of 16 would have required exclusive use. Check which edition your modal or national regulations (ADR, IMDG, ICAO TI, 49 CFR and so on) currently implement, since adoption of the 2025 edition is still in progress.

There is no employee threshold. The GDPR does not tie the obligation to appoint a data protection officer (DPO) to headcount at all.

Under Article 37(1), a controller or processor must appoint a DPO when any of these applies:

- **Public bodies:** the processing is carried out by a public authority or body (courts acting in their judicial capacity are excepted).
- **Large-scale monitoring:** its core activities consist of processing operations that require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale.
- **Large-scale sensitive data:** its core activities consist of large-scale processing of special categories of data (Article 9) or data on criminal convictions and offences (Article 10).

So a five-person company doing large-scale behavioural tracking needs a DPO, while a 5,000-person manufacturer with only routine HR and customer data may not.

Two things often cause the confusion about a number:

- **The 250-employee figure** appears in Article 30(5), which concerns the exemption from keeping records of processing activities, not DPO appointment. An early draft of the GDPR did propose a 250-employee DPO threshold, but it was dropped.
- **National law can add stricter rules.** Article 37(4) lets member states require DPOs in further cases. Germany does this: its Federal Data Protection Act (BDSG, section 38) requires a DPO where, as a rule, at least 20 people are constantly engaged in automated processing of personal data. That threshold was raised from 10 in 2019.

If you're assessing a specific organisation, check the national law of the relevant member state as well as Article 37.

**No. The December 2024 Recommendation is WCAG 2.2 (republished 12 December 2024), and in it 4.1.1 Parsing is marked "Obsolete and removed", so it is not a conformance requirement at any level, including AA.** This is from my knowledge of the document, not a fresh lookup.

**The stated reason:** the note under 4.1.1 explains that the criterion was originally adopted to address problems assistive technology had when directly parsing HTML. Assistive technology no longer needs to parse HTML directly, so those problems either no longer exist or are covered by other criteria. The note concludes that the criterion no longer has utility and is removed.

**For the questionnaire:**
- The accurate answer is "Not applicable: removed in WCAG 2.2", rather than pass or fail.
- If the form only allows pass or fail, "Pass" with a comment citing the removal is the defensible choice. W3C's notes for WCAG 2.0 and 2.1 say 4.1.1 should be treated as always satisfied for HTML or XML content.
- Markup problems that actually affect users, such as duplicate IDs breaking label or ARIA references, are still failures, but under other criteria: typically 1.3.1 Info and Relationships or 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value.

NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 control AC-7 does not prescribe specific numbers. All three values are **organization-defined parameters**, which each organization (or an overlay/baseline it follows) must fill in.

The control text reads, in substance:

- **AC-7a:** Enforce a limit of *[organization-defined number]* consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during an *[organization-defined time period]*.
- **AC-7b:** When that limit is exceeded, automatically take one or more of these actions: lock the account or node for an *[organization-defined time period]*; lock it until released by an administrator; delay the next logon prompt per an *[organization-defined delay algorithm]*; notify the system administrator; or take *[other organization-defined action]*.

So the lockout itself is only one of several permitted responses, and its duration is also left to the organization.

Commonly used values come from frameworks that build on 800-53, not from the control itself:

| Source | Attempts | Time window | Lockout |
|---|---|---|---|
| FedRAMP (Moderate/High) | Not more than 3 | 15 minutes | Minimum 30 minutes (Moderate) or 3 hours (High), or until an administrator unlocks |
| DoD / CNSSI 1253 and many STIGs | 3 | 15 minutes | Until released by an administrator (or a defined period, commonly 15 minutes) |
| NIST SP 800-63B (related guidance for online guessing) | No more than 100 failed attempts per account | Not applicable | Rate limiting, not a fixed lockout |

These figures are from memory and the FedRAMP and DoD parameter values have been revised over time, so check the current baseline that applies to your system before using them in a System Security Plan.

answer:
**11th Edition buffer minimum: 2 seconds.** Section 4I.06 sets a 2-second floor for the steady UPRAISED HAND buffer that separates the pedestrian change interval from the release of conflicting vehicles. Where a red clearance interval is used, its start is the latest point at which the buffer may begin.

**Default walking speed: 3.5 ft/s.** Designers should size the pedestrian clearance time around 3.5 feet per second, so that someone stepping off the curb as WALK ends still reaches the far side of the traveled way or an adequate median. Two adjustments apply:
- **Slower:** A speed below 3.5 ft/s deserves consideration at crosswalks routinely used by slower walkers or wheelchair users.
- **Faster:** Documented engineering judgment can justify evaluating the clearance time at up to 4 ft/s. This wording comes from Missouri DOT's guide, which tracks the MUTCD text.

**2009 MUTCD buffer minimum: 3 seconds.** A 2012 fact sheet quoting the 2009 edition (then Section 4E.06) gives 3 seconds as the buffer minimum ahead of any conflicting vehicular release. The 11th Edition therefore shortened the minimum by one second.

One discrepancy: Missouri DOT's Engineering Policy Guide still shows 3 seconds for the buffer under its Section 4I.06 heading. That is probably a state policy choice, but I did not confirm why it differs from the federal text.
